expectations.text: The reply opens with a clear recommendation the council can act on, without labelling or attacking the alderman.
expectations.evidence: Opens: 'do not advise "yes, in six months" and do not simply say "no"... Advise a gated route instead. The first gate is a legal and impact assessment'. That is actionable. The alderman is not attacked: 'The alderman should hear this now rather than in month five.'

expectations.text: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
expectations.evidence: Names SyRI ('violation of Article 8 ECHR', no reason given), the toeslagenaffaire ('risk models and nationality-based profiling'), Rotterdam ('scored people higher on... gender, language and parenthood') and Amsterdam. Bias is clear, but presumed guilt and the lack of a meaningful human or legal check are not tied to any precedent. One of three. It also gets the Amsterdam date wrong.

expectations.text: The reply questions the "90% accurate" claim: with a low share of real fraud, most people flagged may have done nothing wrong; it asks for false-positive rates and bias tests across groups and proxies such as nationality, age or postcode.
expectations.evidence: 'Only about 15% of flagged people are actual fraudsters, so about 85% of the people investigated are innocent.' 'The vendor must give you precision, recall and false-positive rates at the top-10% cutoff... broken down by group'; 'subgroup fairness metrics (age, gender, nationality, postcode, family type)... Exclude proxies.'

expectations.text: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
expectations.evidence: The GDPR is fully covered: a 'specific statutory basis for each data flow', 'purpose limitation (GDPR Art. 5(1)(b))', 'a DPIA is mandatory and must be completed before processing', 'Art. 22'. The AI Act's Annex III high-risk status and FRIA are covered too. But there is no timing: 'The application dates... have been the subject of postponement proposals (Digital Omnibus). Check the current timeline with legal'. The current 2 December 2027 date is never given.

expectations.text: The reply offers alternatives that address causes, such as simpler rules, help with applications or better data quality, noting that many errors are mistakes rather than fraud.
expectations.evidence: 'Better checks at intake and at changes in circumstances'; 'Investment in error prevention (clear forms, proactive contact), which often recovers more than fraud investigation'; 'Intentional fraud, administrative error and late reporting are very different outcomes.'

expectations.text: The reply sets safeguards for anything that goes ahead: a human decides, people are told and can object, an independent audit, publication in the algorithm register, and criteria for stopping.
expectations.evidence: All five: 'the score may only prioritise a *review*, never trigger a sanction... be able to override'; 'register entry, plain-language notice, objection route'; 'Independent validation' and 'an external review'; 'Stop if the false-positive rate or group disparities are too high', 'a right to stop with no penalty', 'a sunset clause'.

factual_errors.evidence: Amsterdam's 'Smart Check' pilot is said to have been 'halted in 2025 after bias testing' (hedged 'as I understand it... Verify'). It was stopped in late November 2023 (MIT Technology Review, June 2025); 2025 is when it was reported. Other claims check out: Art. 5(1)(d), Art. 27 FRIA, Art. 22, AP prior consultation, and Rotterdam per Lighthouse 2023. Unverified: 'the Algoritmeregister obligation for government' may overstate a policy commitment as a legal duty (web search unavailable).

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of skills, reference files or internal jargon.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt asks for advice on a proposed purchase; no bad outcome has happened yet.

best_insight.value: It turns the alderman's six-month 'live' date into a six-month go/no-go decision date, and advises putting the advice in writing with the legal and DPO opinions attached 'so that the decision and the accountability sit where they belong'.

suggestions.reason: Very thorough (complete safeguards, vendor questions, contract terms), yet it fails the precedent check and the AI Act timing check. Its hedged, wrong Amsterdam date shows why a fact-accuracy check would help.

suggestions.assertion: The reply opens with a clear recommendation the council can act on, without labelling or attacking the alderman.
suggestions.reason: All ten samples pass. Every reply opened with 'advise against' and none attacked the alderman, so this check does not separate samples. A stronger check: the opening gives the alderman something to deliver within six months, not only a 'no'.

suggestions.assertion: The reply names the precedent and what went wrong: the Dutch childcare benefits scandal or similar risk-scoring cases, with bias, presumed guilt and no meaningful human or legal check.
suggestions.reason: The three failure mechanisms are joined by 'and', so it is unclear whether all three are required. I passed samples that tied at least two of the three to a named precedent and failed samples that only named a case or gave one mechanism. Either state that threshold or split the check.

suggestions.assertion: The reply questions the "90% accurate" claim: with a low share of real fraud, most people flagged may have done nothing wrong; it asks for false-positive rates and bias tests across groups and proxies such as nationality, age or postcode.
suggestions.reason: All ten samples pass, so it does not discriminate. Consider checking the arithmetic instead (one sample's '3 to 5 innocent per real case' contradicts its own 5% figures) or requiring named subgroups.

suggestions.assertion: The reply flags the legal floor for counsel: the GDPR (legal basis, purpose limitation for debt-counselling data, a data protection impact assessment, automated decisions) and the AI Act's high-risk rules for public benefits, with their timing.
suggestions.reason: This bundles six items. The 'with their timing' clause did most of the work: two otherwise excellent samples failed only because they did not state the current 2 December 2027 date. Consider splitting the AI Act timing into its own check.

No assertion covers the AI Act Article 5(1)(c) social-scoring prohibition. Debt-counselling data used from an unrelated context is the Commission guidelines' own welfare-fraud example. Five samples raised it and five did not, and it is arguably the most important legal point in this case.

No assertion checks the accuracy of precedent details or dates. For example, one sample put the Amsterdam Smart Check halt in 2025 when it was stopped in late November 2023, and two attributed Algoritmeregister publication to the AI Act.

eval_feedback.overall: Strong safeguards and prevention, but no current AI Act date, precedents not explained beyond bias, and one wrong date: 4/6.
